units.text: We'll compare three ways to express infrastructure without confusing the authoring tool with deployment. SAM uses serverless shorthand. CloudFormation expands the transform and manages the deployed resources. The shorthand doesn't remove the actual I A M or networking requirements.
A local invocation can exercise application behavior. It doesn't prove that the deployed role, network or service integrations work. Use the reviewed deployment to verify these boundaries.

The deployment sends ten percent of alias traffic to the new version during the example canary. The old version handles the rest. Keep clients on the alias: clients pinned directly to a version don't take part in that split.

Watch errors and latency during the canary. The configured CodeDeploy deployment can promote after the interval or roll back if the configured alarm trips. A completed upload is not evidence that the new version behaved well under traffic.
CDK code defines constructs. Synthesis turns them into a template and a cloud assembly. Review what was generated, including permissions and replacements. A successful synthesis isn't a deployment.

Deployment can publish referenced assets and ask CloudFormation to update the stack. Check bootstrap and deployment roles where required. Verify the resulting stack, not just the application's source code.

Choose a direct template for explicit resource definitions, SAM when its serverless shorthand fits, or CDK when you need reusable code constructs. They all reach CloudFormation in the examples here. Whatever you author with, review permissions and changes before execution.

We'll decide where a policy check actually takes effect. A template can be structurally valid and still violate a security rule. Run a separate Guard check. Unless the pipeline gates on its result, that local finding doesn't stop a deployment.

A Guard rule can require that a supported template explicitly declares bucket encryption. That is a check of the template property. It isn't a claim that objects would necessarily be unencrypted without the declaration.

Run both examples: the template with the property should pass, and one omitting it should fail the configured check. Test both to see whether your rule is scoped correctly before relying on it in the pipeline.

A configured CloudFormation Hook can evaluate a supported operation before it proceeds. A failing evaluation in warn mode reports the issue without blocking. In fail mode, the applicable operation can be blocked.
The hook must be active in the right scope and target that operation. Test an expected acceptance and a rejection. A hook configured for one set of actions is not a universal control.

The author defines the change; the pipeline calls the deployment service; the CloudFormation role provisions only what is needed. Give each a separate purpose. A pipeline's ability to update a stack doesn't imply general authority over every resource.
A custom provider runs under its execution role and calls only the required downstream APIs. Scope role passing and the runtime role independently, then verify each role's expected and denied paths.

We'll walk through a safe change rather than assuming a template can preserve application data. Inspect the replacement warning, test an appropriate backup and restore or migration plan, and give the new database an explicit path to the required data.

Before moving clients, verify the data, endpoint, connectivity and workload behavior. A snapshot policy for the old database doesn't populate the replacement by itself. Keep a recovery option until the cutover is verified.

Identify the existing bucket and describe it in the template with the required retention policy. Review an import-only change set. The bucket and its data should stay; the stack now manages that physical resource.
After import, confirm the existing bucket is correctly managed and compare its actual settings with the template. Do any supported configuration changes in a separately reviewed update.

The configured rule rejects an overly broad access setting before CloudFormation is called. Correct it to the explicitly approved network scope and confirm the local validation passes. A configured Hook can still independently check the supported operation before provisioning.

We'll decide where each policy acts. CDK aspects inspect or modify constructs before synthesis. Guard evaluates a template. An active Hook applies at the configured stack operation. Config evaluates deployed resources after the fact.

An organization service control policy sets a permission ceiling for applicable member-account principals. It doesn't grant permissions or replace the other checks. Choose the control that governs the failure you want to prevent or detect.

A deployment-time reference avoids storing the secret value in your template. Rotation can produce a new version, but doesn't automatically make a resource re-read its CloudFormation reference. Check the exact consuming service and refresh path.

For an application that retrieves a secret at runtime, scope the identity and applicable key permissions. Design the cache and refresh behavior to handle rotation. Test that the new value works without logging it.

We'll follow one code revision from a commit to release. Build and test produce an identifiable artifact. If a test fails, stop before promotion. If it passes, keep that same artifact so the release is based on the thing you actually tested.
Release moves through its own checks and may need an approval. Deploy the approved artifact, then verify the environment. A passing build doesn't tell you whether production is healthy.

A Git provider gives you a revision. CodeBuild can turn that revision into a tested artifact. For a container, a registry such as E C R stores the image. The source commit, build result and image digest are related but are not interchangeable identifiers.

CodePipeline coordinates the stages. CodeDeploy can handle supported application deployments, while CloudFormation manages the infrastructure stack. When something fails, identify which action owned the failure before changing a different service.

In the example, development tests a candidate and production receives the same artifact after its gate. Don't rebuild it just before promotion, because the bytes can change. Use the execution record to bind what was tested to what was deployed.

An action can consume an output artifact from an earlier action, and run order governs eligible parallel or sequential work. If approval is rejected or an action fails, inspect that action and artifact before retrying. Rollback follows the configured deployment or pipeline behavior.

CodeBuild runs the configured phases in a build environment. Collect test reports and package the intended output. The build role should read only the inputs and secrets needed to build, not inherit the permissions of the production runtime.
If a command or test fails, inspect the report and logs and stop the artifact's release path. A successful build is still not proof that the deployed environment or integration works.

CodeCommit is again available to new customers. For GitHub, use the approved CodeConnections integration with scoped repository access instead of embedding a personal token. Choose the configured source event for the repository and workflow.

Check that the branch or event you intended starts the pipeline and that its source action reports the expected revision. If the connection is invalid or the event doesn't match, diagnose that boundary instead of embedding alternate credentials.
